Article Title: A Kentucky county closed a 225-acre golf course after it averaged only 9,000 to 10,000 rounds a year; the site is now becoming one of the county’s largest new public parks, with 70% preserved as green
Article Text:
From golf fairways to a 225-acre public park: Kentucky’s former Fox Run Golf Course is getting a new life, with 70% of the property preserved as greenspace.

From golf course to 225-acre public park

Residents can already explore the property

Civic Ridge will focus on families

Adventure Ridge will bring thrills

Trail Ridge will preserve nature

Years of planning behind the transformation

A former golf course in Kentucky is being transformed into a sprawling 225-acre public park featuring hiking and biking trails, climbing structures, a dog park, interactive water features and a potential Go Ape aerial adventure course.According to the August 2026 edition of What’s Happening, the future New Kenton County Park in Independence is expected to break ground in 2026, marking a major new chapter for the former Fox Run Golf Course. County leaders envision the property as a destination where families can spend an entire day exploring, playing and enjoying the outdoors.“This project has always been about creating something completely different from anything else in our region,” Kenton County Judge/Executive Kris Knochelmann said. “We want this park to become a place where families can spend an entire day exploring, playing and making memories.”Located at 604 Independence Station Road in Independence, Kentucky, the property was once home to Fox Run Golf Course. The course averaged only about 9,000 to 10,000 rounds annually, significantly below the roughly 30,000 rounds generally considered necessary for a financially sustainable 18-hole course.In November 2019, Kenton County transitioned management of its golf courses to a third-party operator. As part of the process, officials recommended closing Fox Run to improve the long-term financial sustainability of the county's golf operations.After the closure, the county explored potential redevelopment options and hired CBRE to examine possible future uses for the broader golf course property.Officials eventually discovered that a deed restriction applied to much of the 598-acre property, including the county's other golf courses, Willows and Pioneer. Because the land had originally been acquired using Land and Water Conservation Fund dollars, it was required to remain in recreational use.Rather than leave the former golf course underutilized, the Kenton County Fiscal Court decided to preserve it as public recreational space. In August 2020, the Fiscal Court formally approved converting Fox Run Golf Course into a public park.The property is currently available for passive recreation while the larger development moves forward. Residents can hike, walk, fish, cycle, observe wildlife and explore the natural surroundings.The planned park will preserve much of that natural character. County officials expect approximately 70% of the 225-acre site to remain untouched by construction.The park's design is centered around three distinct ridges - Civic Ridge, Adventure Ridge and Trail Ridge - each offering a different type of experience.Civic Ridge is planned as the park's main gathering and family recreation area.The proposed amenities include improvements to the existing fishing pond, a dog park, an outdoor fitness zone, playground equipment, a shelter house and interactive nature-inspired water features similar to a splash pad.The area will provide spaces where families can gather while remaining connected to the surrounding landscape.For visitors looking for more active experiences, Adventure Ridge will feature outdoor recreation and adventure facilities.Plans include mountain bike trails, a pump track, a climbing wall, additional climbing structures and a potential Go Ape aerial adventure course.Go Ape is known for elevated obstacle courses, zip lines and treetop experiences. If the attraction is finalized, county officials say it would make the park one of only a select number of locations nationwide to offer the experience.The largest of the three ridges will focus on trails, exploration and access to nature.An extensive trail network will wind through the property, while interactive art installations and nature-based experiences are planned to give visitors opportunities to explore the landscape in new ways.The former fairways will therefore have a very different future from their days as a golf course, with much of the land remaining dedicated to natural surroundings and outdoor recreation.The vision for the park began taking shape in 2021, when Kenton County used grant funding to hire Human Nature to develop a comprehensive master plan.The planning process involved extensive community engagement and was divided into three stages: awareness, exploration and vision. Residents and stakeholders were invited to provide input on the site's future and the kinds of amenities they wanted to see.In August 2024, Human Nature was contracted to update the master plan, refine priorities and develop updated cost estimates.J.S. Held was selected in January 2025 as the project's owner's representative, while Bayer Becker joined the team later that year to provide design services. In April 2026, Prus Construction was selected as construction manager.The project team now anticipates breaking ground later in 2026.
Article Summary: A former golf course in Kentucky is being transformed into a 225-acre public park. The New Kenton County Park in Independence is expected to break ground in 2026. The park will feature hiking and biking trails, climbing structures, a dog park, interactive water features and a potential Go Ape aerial adventure course.

Article Title: A couple built a four-bedroom home in Wiltshire for their disabled daughter in 2022, now face council demolition order after planning row over basement and Green Belt rules
Article Text:
A Wiltshire couple face losing the home they built for their disabled daughter after a planning dispute over a basement and Green Belt rules. (Photo: Wiltshire council)

Couple say basement was needed for disabled daughter

Council says house breaches Green Belt policy

Couple call council's approach "harsh and punitive"

Demolition order put on hold

A Wiltshire couple have been ordered to demolish the four-bedroom home they have lived in with their disabled daughter for more than four years after a planning dispute over the property's basement and decking.According to a report published by The Wiltshire Gazette and Herald, Pim and Sheree de Witte built the hillside property at Little Orchard in Kingdown, between Corsham and Bath. The house, which replaced an earlier dwelling on the site, was completed and occupied in 2022.The couple are now appealing to the Planning Inspectorate after Wiltshire Council refused retrospective planning permission for the house as built. The appeal has put the enforcement notice requiring demolition on hold.The de Wittes were originally granted planning permission in 2019 for a replacement dwelling with ground and first-floor levels. However, the completed property included an additional basement level and a decking area.The couple say the basement was constructed as part of the foundations for engineering reasons and was not an arbitrary addition.They subsequently converted the space into residential accommodation for their disabled daughter.They argue that the property remains a replacement dwelling rather than a new-build home and maintain that the original planning permission was lawfully implemented.The couple have also argued that the need to provide suitable accommodation for their disabled daughter should be considered a "material consideration" in the planning decision.The property is located within the Green Belt, and Wiltshire Council has argued that the house as built is materially larger than the dwelling it replaced.A planning application submitted in 2024 seeking to regularise the changes was refused.The couple returned to the council in 2025 with another proposal. Under the revised plans, part of the basement floor area would have been sealed off and concealed by depositing soil around it. The size of the decking would also have been reduced.However, the council rejected the proposal, saying the dwelling remained materially larger than the one it replaced and conflicted with Green Belt policy.The council also said the application failed to demonstrate material considerations or special circumstances that could outweigh the harm identified.The de Wittes have criticised the council's decision, describing its response as "unnecessarily harsh and punitive given the individual circumstances and merits of this case."They have now taken their case to the Planning Inspectorate, which will consider whether the property can remain.The couple have also proposed alternative solutions if their appeal is dismissed, including reinstating the house to its previously approved form.In February this year, the couple were ordered to demolish the property by the end of August. Their appeal has since put that enforcement action on hold while the planning inspector considers the case.The dispute centres on whether the additional basement and decking amount to a breach of the planning permission and whether the circumstances of the family, particularly the accommodation needs of their disabled daughter, provide sufficient grounds for the changes to be retained.A decision from the Planning Inspectorate is expected in the autumn.
Article Summary: Pim and Sheree de Witte built the hillside property at Little Orchard in Kingdown, between Corsham and Bath. The house, which replaced an earlier dwelling on the site, was completed and occupied in 2022. The couple are appealing to the Planning Inspectorate after Wiltshire Council refused retrospective planning permission for the house as built.

Article Title: 15 newborns killed in fire at Islamabad hospital's gynaecology ward in Pakistan
Article Text:
The fire reportedly started after an air-conditioner compressor exploded inside the nursery, according to rescue sources.

15 newborns died after a fire broke out in the gynaecology ward of the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) in Islamabad on Wednesday.According to PIMS officials, the nursery housed 16 newborns when the fire broke out, with only one baby rescued from the ward, reported local outlet Geo News. The fire reportedly started after an air-conditioner compressor exploded inside the nursery, according to rescue officials.The blaze broke out at around 7 am in the gynaecology ward of the hospital, which is located in Pakistan's federal capital. Rescue teams were deployed to the hospital and worked to extinguish the fire and evacuate those inside while carrying out cooling operations at the site.The incident has raised concerns over safety measures in the hospital's neonatal and maternity facilities.
Article Summary: 15 newborns died after a fire broke out in the gynaecology ward of the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) in Islamabad on Wednesday. The fire reportedly started after an air-conditioner compressor exploded inside the nursery, according to rescue sources.

Article Title: US halts visa appointments globally amid Donald Trump's immigration crackdown
Article Text:
Visa appointment schedules will be adjusted to accommodate the training

Immigration crackdown faces legal challenges

Visa revocations add to pressure on applicants

The US has paused visa appointments for applicants around the world as the Trump administration launches a global training programme for consular officers amid its broader immigration crackdown.A US State Department spokesperson said on Tuesday that the department had begun a training initiative at all US embassies and consulates worldwide. Visa appointment schedules will be adjusted to accommodate the training, the spokesperson said, according to Reuters.The State Department did not provide details on the training or specify how long the adjustments would last.It said the programme was aimed at helping consular officers screen applicants who could potentially become dependent on US public benefits and ensure that visa applications are evaluated "comprehensively and consistently".According to a Financial Times report, immigrant visa applicants with scheduled interviews at US embassies and consulates had received emails informing them that their appointments were being rescheduled and that they would be notified of new dates.The development comes as President Donald Trump's administration continues a broad immigration crackdown that has included visa and green-card revocations and the rejection of applications on various grounds, including political opinions and participation in pro-Palestinian protests.Trump has said the crackdown is intended to improve domestic security.The administration's immigration policies have also faced legal setbacks. A US judge on Friday struck down a policy that suspended the issuance of immigrant visas to applicants from 75 countries, ruling that the measure exceeded secretary of state Marco Rubio's statutory authority.The administration has also moved to tighten restrictions on legal immigration.The US Department of Homeland Security has proposed making permanent a $103,265 fee for new cap-subject H-1B visa petitions, after a previous $100,000 fee imposed by Trump was blocked by a court.The proposed fee would significantly increase the cost for employers hiring foreign workers in specialised fields.The H-1B programme allows US employers to hire foreign workers with specialised training. The programme provides 65,000 visas annually, along with another 20,000 for workers with advanced degrees.Trump's administration has also ordered enhanced vetting of H-1B applicants and proposed changes to the visa selection process that would favour higher-skilled and better-paid workers.The administration is separately preparing to revoke the business and tourism visas of potentially up to 200,000 foreigners who have applied for or are currently seeking asylum in the US.The proposed action would cover B1 and B2 visas issued between 2016 and 2026 whose holders have sought or are seeking asylum. The State Department is expected to announce the move in the coming weeks, according to news agency AP.B1 visas are generally issued for business travel, while B2 visas are generally used for tourism, family visits or medical treatment.The administration has also tightened screening requirements for visa applicants, including demands for additional information about their social media histories and, in some cases, expensive visa bonds.The latest pause in appointments therefore comes as the Trump administration continues to review and tighten several aspects of the US immigration and visa system.
Article Summary: US State Department has begun a training initiative at all US embassies and consulates worldwide. Visa appointment schedules will be adjusted to accommodate the training, a spokesperson said. The State Department did not provide details on the training or specify how long the adjustments would last. The development comes as the Trump administration continues a broad immigration crackdown.

Article Title: Singapore sends 70 tonnes of unwanted clothes to Malaysia every week in major textile recycling partnership
Article Text:
Image: CNA/YouTube

How Singapore’s unwanted clothes reach a recycling facility in Malaysia

What happens to the clothes after they arrive in Malaysia

Why the 70-tonne weekly flow matters for textile waste

Singapore is sending up to 70 tonnes of unwanted clothing to Malaysia every week under a cross-border textile recycling partnership designed to give discarded garments a second life. The initiative involves social enterprise Cloop, which collects unwanted clothes through its textile recycling bins before sending them to Life Line Clothing in Port Klang, Malaysia. The volume being shipped is now twice what it was two years ago, highlighting both the growing scale of the operation and the enormous challenge of managing textile waste. At Life Line Clothing’s facility, the collected garments are sorted to determine whether they can be reused, recycled or processed into other materials. The arrangement is intended to keep more textiles in circulation and reduce the amount of clothing ultimately sent for disposal.The journey begins with textile collection points across Singapore. Cloop, a social enterprise focused on textile circularity, operates recycling bins where members of the public can deposit unwanted clothing. Instead of treating these garments as ordinary household waste, the collection system channels them into a sorting and recovery process.The scale of the operation has grown substantially. According to CNA, Singapore now sends up to 70 tonnes of unwanted clothing to Life Line Clothing in Malaysia every week, around twice the amount shipped through the arrangement two years ago. The increase demonstrates how a collection network can move significant quantities of discarded textiles across borders for further processing. Once the clothing reaches Port Klang, it enters Life Line Clothing’s textile recovery operation. Garments are assessed and separated according to their condition and material, allowing usable items and recyclable textiles to follow different pathways. The cross-border model also reflects the practical challenges of textile recycling in a densely populated city. Clothing can contain blends of fibres, dyes, buttons, zips and other components that make straightforward recycling difficult. Sorting is therefore an important stage in determining whether a garment can be worn again or needs to be processed into another form.At Life Line Clothing’s facility in Port Klang, the collected garments are sorted for reuse and recycling. The objective is to identify clothing that still has value as a wearable item while directing damaged or unsuitable textiles towards material recovery. CNA visited the Malaysian facility to examine what happens to the clothing after it leaves Singapore. Reuse is generally the simplest way to extend a garment’s life because it keeps the existing product in circulation without requiring the fabric to be broken down and manufactured again. Clothing that cannot be reused can instead enter recycling streams, where fibres and materials may be recovered for other applications. The process illustrates why simply placing unwanted clothing into a collection bin does not necessarily mean every item will become a new garment. Textile recovery involves multiple stages, and the final destination depends heavily on the condition, composition and quality of each item. For Singapore, however, diverting clothing into a dedicated recovery system creates an opportunity to manage textiles as a resource rather than immediately treating them as waste. The growing volume being handled by the partnership suggests that more unwanted garments are entering this recovery pathway.In practice, only about half of the clothing that arrives at the facility is resold, typically compressed into bales and shipped to wholesalers in overseas secondhand markets such as Kenya, Uganda and Papua New Guinea. The remaining half is repurposed into rags or industrial wiping cloths rather than reused as garments. Items that cannot be reused or repurposed in any form are, as a last resort, incinerated to generate electricity.The partnership comes against a wider challenge facing cities around the world, the environmental impact of discarded clothing. Textile production requires raw materials, water, energy and manufacturing resources, while discarded garments can represent a significant loss of those resources when they are not reused or recovered. The Singapore-Malaysia arrangement attempts to address part of this problem by extending the useful life of textiles. Sending as much as 70 tonnes of clothing each week for recovery creates a large-scale route through which garments can be sorted, reused or recycled rather than simply discarded. The fact that the volume has doubled compared with two years earlier is also significant. It could indicate that more people are using textile collection points, that larger quantities of clothing are being collected, or that the recovery partnership has expanded its capacity. Nevertheless, there is more to cutting down the wastage than merely recycling the waste. The lifespan of the fabrics can be extended through reuse and repairs and the responsible purchase of new clothes. It thus means that the process of creating a successful circular system will require not only the collection but also changes to the way in which clothes are produced, purchased, used, and discarded. One such example of an organization working to recover waste textiles is the collaboration between Cloop and Life Line Clothing. Through the transportation of 70 tonnes of unwanted clothes per week from Singapore to the processing facility in Malaysia, the project creates a huge recovery pathway for the fabrics that would have ended up as waste.
Article Summary: Singapore is sending up to 70 tonnes of unwanted clothing to Malaysia every week under a cross-border textile recycling partnership. The initiative involves social enterprise Cloop, which collects unwanted clothes through its textile recycling bins before sending them to Life Line Clothing in Port Klang, Malaysia. At the facility, the collected garments are sorted to determine whether they can be reused, recycled or processed into other materials.

Article Title: Port Houston donates $500,000 to 32 nonprofits, supporting workforce training, STEM education and community projects
Article Text:
Image: Business Wire

32 organisations receive funding for education, health, food and environmental projects

Nearly half of the funding is aimed at building the region’s future workforce

Port Houston shifts future grants towards community-identified priorities

Port Houston has awarded $500,000 in Community Grants to 32 organisations serving communities across the Houston Ship Channel region. The funding will support programmes ranging from workforce training and STEM education to healthcare access, food assistance, environmental projects and neighbourhood improvements. According to Port Houston press release distributed via Business Wire, the latest grant cycle attracted 194 applications requesting more than $6.6 million, highlighting the scale of demand for community investment. Nearly half of the funding awarded this year is dedicated to workforce development, with supported programmes helping students explore career paths, earn industry-recognised credentials and develop skills for maritime, logistics and industrial careers. Since launching the Community Grants Programme in 2020, Port Houston has invested more than $2.15 million in local organisations. The 2026 awards also mark a transition, with future grants from 2027 set to follow priorities identified through Port Houston’s Anchored in Action Community Investment Plan.The 32 grant recipients represent a broad cross-section of community initiatives. Armand Bayou Nature Center received $15,000 for school field-trip access, while the Barbara Bush Houston Literacy Foundation received $25,000 for East End community STEM literacy initiatives.Baytown Habitat for Humanity was awarded $15,000 for its Safe and Stable Homes Repair & Resilience Initiative, and Art League of Baytown received $7,250 for its Arts and the Ship Channel programme. Compudopt received $25,000 for its Pathways Programme, while Galena Park Resource and Training Center was awarded $25,000 for community learning and engagement. Lee College Foundation received $20,000 for logistics software expansion, linking education directly to one of the region’s major employment sectors. The grants also address health, food security and access to essential services. Kids' Meals received $15,000 for healthy meal delivery, Second Servings of Houston received $20,000 to expand access to nutritious food, and Target Hunger was awarded $12,750 for food assistance and navigation. Ronald McDonald House Charities Greater Houston received $20,000 for its Care Mobile, while The Rose received $25,000 for its Empower Her Health programme. Other awards support environmental education and neighbourhood improvement, including $15,000 for Citizens' Environmental Coalition, $5,000 for Greens Bayou Coalition and $10,000 for Fit Houston’s Mason Park revitalisation project.Workforce development emerged as one of the strongest priorities in the 2026 grant round, accounting for nearly half of the funding. Port Houston said the supported programmes will help residents explore career pathways, gain industry-recognised credentials and develop skills relevant to maritime, logistics and industrial sectors that underpin the regional economy. Several recipients are directly focused on career preparation. SERJobs received $20,000 for its Building the Port Workforce Initiative, Women Offshore Foundation received $25,000 for career development, and the Prison Entrepreneurship Program received $15,000 for workforce and entrepreneurship empowerment. Career-focused projects also include Friends of Galena Park Branch Library’s $2,500 Career Exploration and Resume Hub and Friends of Pasadena Public Library’s $5,000 programme connecting residents with pathways into industrial construction. Education is another major component. La Porte Independent School District received $15,000 for Elementary STEM Academies, designed to provide hands-on experiences that encourage curiosity, innovation, critical thinking, creativity and collaboration. Houston Symphony Society received $10,000 for its Student Concert Series, while Segundo Barrio Children's Chorus received $20,000 for its community programme. These investments reflect an effort to build skills and opportunities from childhood through adulthood.The 2026 awards come as Port Houston prepares to change how its Community Grants Programme is shaped. Beginning in 2027, future investments will be guided by priorities identified through its Anchored in Action Community Investment Plan. The plan was developed using input from more than 10,000 residents across 14 communities located near the port. The change is intended to ensure future investments more closely reflect needs and opportunities identified by residents themselves. That approach builds on the programme’s existing emphasis on expanding opportunity, addressing community needs and strengthening neighbourhoods connected to the Houston Ship Channel. The latest round also demonstrates how much demand exists among local organisations. The 194 applications submitted in 2026 collectively requested more than $6.6 million, meaning the $500,000 available represented only a portion of the funding sought. Port Houston said the applications demonstrated both the significant needs in the region and the commitment of nonprofits, schools and community partners working to address them. Since 2020, Port Houston has invested more than $2.15 million through the programme. The port also plays a major economic role beyond its grant-making activities, its Houston Ship Channel complex includes more than 200 private and eight public terminals and supports nearly 1.5 million jobs in Texas and 3.37 million nationwide, according to the announcement. The latest grants connect that economic presence with direct investment in education, employment, health, food access, environmental stewardship and neighbourhood development.
Article Summary: 32 organisations receive funding for education, health, food and environmental projects. Nearly half of the funding is aimed at building the region’s future workforce. The 2026 awards come as Port Houston prepares to change how its Community Grants Programme is shaped. Beginning in 2027, future investments will be guided by priorities identified by the port.

Article Title: 'Warned by FBI, Canadian police of credible plot': SFJ's Pannun claims fresh threat to life
Article Text:
Khalistani terrorist Gurpatwant Pannun

Also Read |

Khalistani terrorist Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, a dual US-Canadian citizen, claimed on Tuesday (local time) that he had been warned by both the FBI and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) of a “new credible threat” to his life.Pannun, the general counsel of Sikhs For Justice (SFJ), said FBI agents visited him last Thursday and advised him not to travel until the threat was resolved. He added that the agency asked him to notify them in advance if he did make any travel plans.“I was warned under the terms of a ‘Duty to Warn’ law in the United States,” Pannun told the Associated Press, referring to a provision that requires US intelligence and law enforcement agencies to alert individuals when they become aware of credible and specific threats involving murder, serious bodily harm or kidnapping.“I’m not afraid of their death threats. I’m going to continue, even at the cost of a bullet,” Pannun said.His remarks came after he claimed that the RCMP had also warned him by telephone on Tuesday. Neither law enforcement agency, however, disclosed details of the alleged plot or threat.Pannun further stated that Canadian law enforcement officials had issued similar “Duty to Warn” advisories to Hardeep Singh Nijjar, another Khalistani terrorist and a Canadian citizen, in the weeks leading up to his assassination in Surrey, Canada, in June 2023.Nijjar’s killing had triggered a major diplomatic row between Canada and India after the then-Justin Trudeau government alleged that the Indian government was involved in the assassination. New Delhi rejected the allegations.In a separate case , Indian national Nikhil Gupta pleaded guilty in February to federal conspiracy charges over a 2023 plot to assassinate Pannun. Gupta is awaiting sentencing, scheduled for November 20, in a Manhattan federal court.Federal sentencing guidelines recommend that Gupta serve at least 20 years in prison.
Article Summary: Khalistani terrorist Gurpatwant Singh Pannun claims he has been warned of a 'new credible threat' to his life. The dual US-Canadian citizen claims he was warned by both the FBI and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) Neither law enforcement agency disclosed details of the alleged plot or threat.

Article Title: Mojtaba Khamenei seen, heard in rare video amid health concerns
Article Text:
Mojtaba seen, heard in an undated video

Reports of ‘extremely critical’ condition

Mojtaba’s low public profile

A new video of Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has surfaced amid growing mystery over his health, appearance and whereabouts.According to Al Arabiya, Iran’s Fars News released archival footage showing Mojtaba Khamenei surrounded by a group of people who offered prayers before beginning their discussions.The footage comes amid repeated claims by US President Donald Trump that Mojtaba is in "bad shape" and was "seriously injured" following the strikes that killed his father Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, Iran’s longest-serving Supreme Leader.This is the second video of Mojtaba Khamenei to emerge in August. The footage, however, is undated.It is also the first video in which his voice can be clearly heard. The video showed Mojtaba presiding religious academic discussion with clerics.The video was first published by Mehr, a semi-official Iranian news agency sponsored by the government and run by the Islamic Development Organisation. Its release appeared aimed at countering growing speculation about Mojtaba’s health and whereabouts.The video surfaced after reports in Israeli media claimed that Mojtaba Khamenei was in an "extremely critical condition".Israel’s Channel 14, citing sources inside Iran, and an earlier report by The Jerusalem Post, quoting IranWire and sources close to Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian ’s administration, said concerns about Mojtaba’s health were circulating within Iran’s leadership.Iranian officials have rejected the reports.President Masoud Pezeshkian said Mojtaba Khamenei was "completely healthy", dismissing speculation about his physical condition, according to Iran’s ISNA news agency."Someone who can sit and discuss for seven to eight hours cannot have any health problems," Pezeshkian said, adding that he had held a "very good" meeting with Mojtaba earlier in August.Mojtaba Khamenei became Iran’s Supreme Leader after his father Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, was killed in joint US-Israeli military strikes on February 28.Since taking over, Mojtaba has largely remained out of public view.Unlike previous Iranian leaders, he has not made public appearances and has communicated mainly through written statements.
Article Summary: Mojtaba Khamenei seen, heard in an undated video. Reports in Israeli media claimed he was in an "extremely critical condition" US President Donald Trump said Mojtaba is in "bad shape" and was "seriously injured"

Article Title: US diplomats heading back to Middle East as immediate Iran war risk recedes: Report
Article Text:
US to restore staffing at Middle East embassies after Iran war evacuations, NYT report

The United States is preparing to return diplomats to several Middle Eastern embassies that were evacuated during the war with Iran, according to a report by the New York Times. The move suggests Washington does not expect a return to full-scale fighting in the immediate future.According to an internal State Department document cited by NYT, Foreign Service officers could begin returning to their posts as early as this week. The plan covers US diplomatic missions in Israel, Lebanon, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Jordan, Oman, Iraq and Kuwait.The US Embassy in Lebanon is expected to be the first to receive returning diplomats, although it will continue operating below full staffing. Under the plan, staffing would eventually return to full strength in Israel, Jordan and Oman.Embassies in the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Lebanon would initially operate at up to 85% staffing, while missions in Iraq, Kuwait and Bahrain would be capped at 75%.The State Department said it was continually reviewing security conditions at its diplomatic missions and adjusting staffing levels to allow the US to pursue its foreign-policy objectives while protecting personnel.The planned return comes despite the fact that US-Iran talks have stalled and Washington has continued to increase economic pressure on Tehran.The US announced a fresh round of sanctions on August 24 targeting Iranian military activities, procurement networks, cyber operations and petroleum trade.The decision to bring diplomats back nevertheless represents a significant shift from earlier this year. The US began reducing its diplomatic presence in the region after tensions with Iran escalated in February, with nonessential personnel and family members evacuated from several posts. Some embassies were subsequently hit or targeted by drones and rockets during the conflict.Former US officials said the redeployment could indicate that Washington believes the immediate risk of renewed fighting has fallen. But they cautioned that it should not be interpreted as proof of a lasting peace. Restrictions on family members at several Gulf missions also suggest that the State Department continues to see an elevated security threat.The move is less a declaration that the Iran conflict is over and more a signal that Washington believes its diplomats can begin returning while the fragile post-war standoff continues.
Article Summary: Diplomats could begin returning to their posts as early as this week, according to an internal State Department document. The plan covers US diplomatic missions in Israel, Lebanon, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Jordan, Oman, Iraq and Kuwait. The US Embassy in Lebanon is expected to be the first to receive returning diplomats.

Article Title: US removes Syria from terrorism list after 46 years - what it means for the Middle East country
Article Text:
Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa said in a video message that Syria is ‘shaking off a dark burden’ (File photo)

The United States on Monday removed Syria from its list of state sponsors of terrorism, ending a designation that had been in place since 1979 and imposing significant restrictions on trade, investment and financial transactions with the country.The move, which followed a 45-day congressional review, marks a further step in Washington’s efforts to deepen ties with Syria’s new government under President Ahmed al-Sharaa. The US also revoked the designation of the Nusrah Front, later known as Hay’at Tahrir al-Sham (HTS), as a Specially Designated Global Terrorist organisation. The Treasury Department announced corresponding sanctions relief.“These actions were all taken in recognition of the positive actions taken and further commitments by the Syrian government under President Ahmed al-Sharaa to fully distance Syria from acts of international terrorism,” US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement.Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the measures would encourage investment and support Syria’s economic recovery. “Today's action will help foster additional investment in Syria to promote political and economic stability,” he said.The Treasury said the changes were “in line with President (Donald) Trump's promise to deliver sanctions relief to Syria”. It added that the removal of the restrictions “does not change Treasury's posture with regards to countering global terrorism and our commitment to hold bad actors in Syria accountable.”The state sponsor designation had remained a major obstacle for businesses and financial institutions considering investment in Syria, even after the US ended its broader sanctions programme against the country in July 2025. The designation restricted US foreign assistance, defence exports and sales, certain dual-use goods and financial transactions.The Treasury has since said US financial institutions can provide services to Syria, process payments involving Syrian banks and establish correspondent banking relationships, provided sanctioned entities are not involved.Syria’s government welcomed Monday’s decision, describing it as an opportunity to reconnect with the global financial system and attract investment needed for reconstruction after nearly 14 years of war.Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shibani had earlier called the terrorism designation the “last obstacle” to rebuilding economic ties. “There is no longer any obstacle to investment, doing business and rebuilding economic life in Syria,” he said.The US designation had been imposed in 1979, when Washington accused the government of then-President Hafez al-Assad of supporting militant groups. It continued under his son Bashar al-Assad, who was overthrown by rebels led by Sharaa in December 2024.HTS, formerly known as the Nusrah Front, was once affiliated with al Qaeda in Syria before breaking ties with the group in 2016. Sharaa later led the rebel coalition that toppled Assad and became president.With Syria’s removal, Cuba, Iran and North Korea remain the three countries on the US state sponsors of terrorism list.The latest decision follows a broader rapprochement between Washington and Damascus. US President Donald Trump has backed sanctions relief for Syria and met Sharaa during a visit to Turkey, as the new Syrian government seeks international support for economic reconstruction.Syrian officials have also been pursuing closer links with international financial institutions and companies. The country's finance ministry has held discussions with Bank of America executives, while Mastercard has announced work with QNB Group and Syria’s central bank to develop infrastructure for international card payments.Washington has said its engagement with Damascus is aimed at supporting Syria’s stabilisation, economic recovery and reintegration into the global economy, while maintaining targeted measures against terrorism and other sanctioned actors.
Article Summary: US removes Syria from its list of state sponsors of terrorism. The designation had been in place since 1979 and imposed significant restrictions on trade, investment and financial transactions with the country. The US also revoked the designation of the Nusrah Front, later known as Hay’at Tahrir al-Sham.

Article Title: 'Lake America': Trump floats plan to rename Lake Ontario amid escalating US-Canada trade row
Article Text:
Trump said US is considering to change the name of Lake Ontario.

Carney rejects US trade demands

Trade tensions deepen

Trump, Ontario premier trade barbs

Auto industry at centre of dispute

President Donald Trump on Tuesday said the United States was “giving serious consideration” to renaming Lake Ontario as Lake America, amid escalating trade dispute with Canada.In a post on Truth Social, Trump wrote, “The United States is giving serious consideration to changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America in that we don’t expect to doing much business with Ontario any longer. Thank you for your attention to this matter!”Trump's remark came amid a growing war of words between Washington and Ottawa after Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney walked away from trade negotiations with the Trump administration late Friday. The move was followed by Trump's threatened 50% tariffs on about $20 billion worth of Canadian goods.Trump also pushed back against Carney's comments on French-language protections in Canada, saying in another Truth Social post, saying, “I would never interfere with Canadians speaking French! In fact, I have never even thought of doing such a stupid thing."“This lie was made up by a weak and ineffective Prime Minister in an attempt to gain political support, which he has totally lost, from the people of Quebec. I love French Canadians!” he added.Canada is preparing retaliatory tariffs against the US as the dispute widened. Trump had earlier told Canadian leaders to “fall in line” or face consequences “far worse” than existing tariffs, while Carney accused Washington of trying to subordinate Canada.Trump has also threatened 50% tariffs on Canadian vehicles, auto parts and steel. Carney said the US proposals would damage key Canadian industries.“We learned during the negotiations that the Americans want to destroy our major industries, including autos, steel and aluminum,” Carney said. “That was one of the main reasons we said no. It was a bad deal.”Carney said Canada would not accept “an attitude at the negotiation table that Canada is a subsidiary of the United States” and indicated that Ottawa could move away from matching US tariffs dollar for dollar, instead focusing on targeted measures to protect Canadian workers and businesses.He also criticised Washington's position on French-language and cultural protections, saying US negotiators viewed the French language as an “irritant”.“For Americans, French language, Francophone culture, Canadian culture, these are irritants,” Carney said in French at a news conference in Quebec. “Here in Quebec, here in Canada, these are rights.”The dispute threatens one of the world's largest trading relationships, with the US and Canada closely linked through supply chains in automobiles, energy, agriculture and manufacturing.Carney questioned Washington's reliability as a trading partner, saying Canada was finding reliable partners “everywhere in the world, except in the United States. Except in the United States. And Russia.”Trump, meanwhile, accused Canada of exploiting the US and criticised its tariffs on American agricultural products. He has also warned that tariffs on Canada's auto industry could take effect next year.Carney said the proposed US auto measures could gradually dismantle Canadian vehicle production, calling the existing cross-border industry “the most successful automotive partnership in history.”Ontario Premier Doug Ford has also joined the confrontation, saying Canadians were prepared to bear economic costs rather than give in to US pressure.“We’re all in,” Ford told The Associated Press. “Up here, we’re at a fever pitch; everyone’s in for an economic war. They know they’re going to have to sacrifice.”Trump responded by attacking Ford personally, calling him “the less charismatic, intelligent, and overall unimpressive brother of the late, great, Rob Ford,” and again referring to Carney as “Governor Carney”.Ford dismissed the remarks, saying, “If you think an insult from him hurts me? Well, bring it on, buddy, I’m ready.”Despite political differences between Ford's Progressive Conservative Party and Carney's Liberal Party, the dispute has underscored broad political opposition in Canada to Trump's trade demands.Ford warned that Ontario could take further measures if the dispute worsens, including restricting electricity and critical mineral supplies to the US.“We power 1.5 million homes and businesses,” Ford said. “Everything’s on the table. I’ll do whatever it takes.”He has previously used electricity exports as leverage, with Ontario imposing a 25% surcharge on electricity supplied to Michigan, Minnesota and New York during an earlier phase of the dispute.Ford also accused Trump of seeking to weaken Canadian industries and shift production to the US.“He wants to bleed out every single sector and bring them down to the US,” Ford said.The automotive sector has emerged as one of the biggest flashpoints. Ontario is the centre of Canada's vehicle manufacturing industry, with major automakers including Ford, General Motors and Stellantis operating plants in the province.The industry is deeply integrated with US manufacturing, with auto parts crossing the border multiple times during production. Trump's threat of 50% tariffs on Canadian vehicles and parts could therefore affect manufacturers and workers on both sides of the border.US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer defended Washington's position, saying “the only reason Canada has auto production in the first place” was the 1960s Auto Pact, under which Canada used access to its market to encourage vehicle production.Ford also said he had opposed a preliminary trade agreement being considered by Carney and rejected the idea of restoring American liquor to Ontario stores as part of a deal.“I wasn’t going to put the booze back on the shelves,” Ford said. “I was ready to go out there and call a press conference … and say I’m not buckling over.”The dispute has also raised concerns over Canadian sovereignty after Carney said Washington had sought language that could restrict Canada's ability to negotiate trade agreements with other countries.
Article Summary: President Donald Trump said the United States was “giving serious consideration” to renaming Lake Ontario as Lake America. Trump's remark came amid a growing war of words between Washington and Ottawa. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney walked away from trade negotiations with the Trump administration late Friday.

Article Title: From Gen Z wave to heat in 150 days: Balen faces street anger, parl pressure and party unease
Article Text:
Nepal PM Balen Shah faces protests, Parliament heat and RSP dissent

Barely 150 days after Gen Z anger helped propel Balendra “Balen” Shah to Nepal’s top job, the same restless street energy that propelled his rise seems to be pinning him down, leaving the former rapper and Kathmandu mayor under pressure from public protests, Parliament and his own Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP).Barely two months after he took office, young protesters returned to Kathmandu’s Maitighar Mandala demanding his resignation, while opposition MPs attacked his repeated absence from Parliament, where he attended only five of the first 39 sittings before Speaker Dol Prasad Aryal directed him to appear and answer lawmakers on Aug 26.The political honeymoon began fraying within weeks of Shah taking office on March 27 after RSP swept 182 of 275 House seats. In April, strict enforcement of customs rules on goods brought across the open India border hit people dependent on Indian markets for groceries, medicines and household essentials, triggering protests in border towns and forcing authorities to relax the move.Public anger intensified in July after 25-year-old ride-share driver Ganesh Nepali self-immolated outside the passport office in Kathmandu following a dispute over municipal action against his vehicle.His death fuelled demonstrations over municipal policing and revived criticism of drives against informal settlements and landless squatters without adequate rehabilitation.Shah also faced sustained attacks over Nepal’s border dispute with India after telling Parliament, “After becoming PM, I came to know that not only has India encroached on Nepal’s land, but Nepal has also encroached on India’s land.” Opposition parties demanded evidence, withdrawal of the statement and an apology.Pressure also came from Nepal’s media fraternity. Federation of Nepali Journalists (FNJ) alleged in May that senior journalist Kishore Shrestha faced police surveillance, an attempted arrest and threats after his publication carried reports critical of a minister and ruling-party leaders.Violent communal clashes in southern Nepal along the border with India added another layer of pressure and forced Shah to address the nation after criticism over his delayed response, while in Pokhara former Gorkha servicemen, their families and prospective recruits continued demanding a resolution of stalled recruitment of Nepalis into Indian Army under Agnipath.The strain meanwhile has spread inside RSP, where lawmakers and senior leaders questioned Shah’s distance from party structures and unilateral governing style, with party insiders saying he had shown “little faith in the party system itself”. RSP MP Jagadish Kharel sharpened the criticism from within while speaking in Parliament, saying, “This govt will not survive if only the dignity of the Prime Minister is preserved. Our dignity must also be preserved”.The unease was serious enough for home minister Sudan Gurung to urge colleagues at RSP’s Aug 19 parliamentary-party discussion to "contain" their differences rather than carry them into House. “Let’s keep the quarrels at home, let’s not oppose (the govt) in the House; the opposition is beginning to grow stronger,” he said.
Article Summary: Nepal PM Balen Shah under pressure from public protests, Parliament and his own Rastriya Swatantra Party. Young protesters returned to Kathmandu’s Maitighar Mandala demanding his resignation. Opposition MPs attacked his repeated absence from Parliament.

Article Title: 12-year-old hailed ‘hero’ for calling 911 before Montana gunman killed her, 7 others
Article Text:
Police said they responded to the home on Sunday evening and heard gunshots coming from out back, just before the house was completely engulfed in flames. (Photo: AP)

Victims spanned four generations

Officers heard shots before flames engulfed house

Family moved to Montana from Seattle area

Relative says there were ‘many red flags’

Montana case is 22nd US mass killing this year

Husband raced home after hearing shooting alert

Fire damage complicates investigation

A 12-year-old girl called 911 from inside a Montana home as a gunman killed eight relatives, including four children, during a Sunday family dinner outside Billings. The victims belonged to four generations of the same blended family.Charlotte Ghekiere, 12, was among those killed. Family friend Jennifer Mercer said the girl called 911 and tried to save her relatives, something the family wanted made public. “The one thing we do know is that Charlotte was the hero,” Mercer said.The gunman was identified by relative Brad Ireland as Alan Smith, 44. Smith had lived with his parents for years before they asked him to leave a couple of weeks earlier, but he returned unexpectedly on Sunday evening as relatives gathered for their regular family dinner and opened fire, Ireland said, according to news agency Associated Press.The oldest victim was Smith’s grandmother, Evelyn Smith, who was in her 90s, used a wheelchair and lived in a nearby retirement community. The youngest was 7-year-old Chloe Ireland.Smith’s parents, Dana and Barb Smith, and his younger sister, Megan Ghekiere, were also killed. Megan’s children with former husband Brad Ireland, Owen Ireland, 13, and Chloe, were among the four children who died.Her two stepchildren with current husband Adam Ghekiere, Landon Ghekiere, 15, and Charlotte, 12, were also killed.Mercer, who was authorized to release information about the victims, later launched an online appeal to help the family meet funeral and other expenses.She described the family as close and loving, saying the children got along and their parents remained amicable even after divorcing. She also said the deaths had devastated the wider community, including people who had never known the family.Officers arrived at the property on Sunday evening and heard gunshots from the rear of the house. Soon afterwards, flames engulfed the building.Investigators confirmed on Tuesday that eight people had been killed, including four children. They also said the suspect had suffered a self-inflicted gunshot wound and later died. Ireland said Smith killed his grandmother, parents, younger sister and the four children before setting the house on fire. He added that Smith tried to flee before encountering law enforcement.Firefighters could not immediately tackle the blaze because authorities first had to secure the scene. Once they were able to enter the area, crews continued fighting the fire until about 1am on Monday, Billings Fire Department Chief Matt Hoppel said.The subdivision is outside Billings city limits and is not required to have fire hydrants. The delay in starting firefighting operations gave the flames additional time to spread through the house.The family originally came from the Seattle area. After Ireland and Megan divorced six years ago, she moved to Montana with their children, where she later met Adam Ghekiere, who became her second husband.Her parents, Dana and Barb Smith, subsequently followed her to Montana and settled in Billings nearby. Dana’s elderly mother, Evelyn, lived separately in a retirement community in the area, Ireland said.Alan Smith had also been living in Montana with his parents for several years before they recently asked him to leave. He returned to their home on Sunday evening while relatives were gathering for their regular family meal.Adam Ghekiere was at work and was not at the house when the shooting occurred.Ireland, who lives in Arizona and lost his former wife and two children in the shooting, said there had been warning signs involving Smith.“There were many red flags and many people spoke out,” he said. “No one listened.”He described Smith as a “hermit” who generally remained in his room and spent much of his time on a computer. Ireland said relatives did not know what he did there throughout the day.Smith attended Eastern Washington University but had been unable to find a job or keep one. Criminal-record checks in Montana and Washington also found no previous arrest or criminal charge involving him.Ireland said he was unaware of any previous violence by Smith, although he said his former brother-in-law could be verbally abusive.Friends of the victims have since created two GoFundMe campaigns to support Adam Ghekiere and his former wife, Erica Schneider.The case is the 22nd US mass killing recorded this year by a database compiled by the news agency and USA Today with Northeastern University. Of those incidents, 15 stemmed from domestic disputes.James Alan Fox, the Northeastern University criminologist responsible for the database, said domestic disputes account for about half of US mass killings on average.No US mass killing since April has had a higher death toll. In that earlier Louisiana case, a father killed eight children, seven of them his own, and wounded his wife and another woman.Adam Ghekiere was working at the Billings airport when he heard a report of an active shooting over a dispatch radio. He immediately called each member of his family before driving across Billings to the Smith home.By the time he arrived, the house was already ablaze. About two hours later, he learned that his wife and children had been killed.Ghekiere said he had not expected his children to be at the gathering because the family normally held its dinner on Fridays. Their presence that Sunday also led him to believe Smith had not expected to find them there.“I don’t think he expected my kids to be there,” he said, referring to his brother-in-law.Police later told Ghekiere that Charlotte had made the emergency call from inside the house. As he recalled his daughter, he said one particular exchange continued to stay with him.“I keep hearing her quote to me every time I would say ‘I love you’ and she would say ‘I love you more,’” he said.The fire burned the house to its foundation, leaving investigators with concerns about the structural integrity of what remained. Those concerns have complicated the investigation, Billings Police Department spokesperson Jeff Stovall said.
Article Summary: Alan Smith, 44, killed his grandmother, parents, younger sister and four children before setting the house on fire. Family friend Jennifer Mercer said the girl called 911 and tried to save her relatives, something the family wanted made public. Police said they responded to the home on Sunday evening and heard gunshots coming from out back, just before the house was completely engulfed in flames.

Article Title: Watch: US military's 'lethal kinetic strike' destroys suspected drug boat in Caribbean; 4 killed
Article Text:
The US military has described those targeted as “narcoterrorists”

At least 227 killed in boat strikes

Trump administration expands anti-cartel campaign

The US military carried out a strike on a boat suspected of being involved in drug trafficking in the Caribbean Sea on Tuesday, killing four people, as the Trump administration continues its campaign against alleged drug traffickers in Latin America.The US Southern Command posted a video of the operation on X, showing what appeared to be a moving boat followed by a flash after the strike.The military said intelligence had confirmed the vessel was actively involved in drug trafficking, but did not release evidence supporting the claim or provide the identities of those killed.Southern Command said on X, “Joint Task Force Western Hemisphere executed a lethal kinetic strike on a go-fast vessel operating along established narco-trafficking routes in the Caribbean. Confirmed intelligence revealed the vessel's active involvement in narco-trafficking. The operation killed four narco-terrorists.” It said the vessel was operating along established narco-trafficking routes in the Caribbean.The latest attack comes just two days after the US military struck another vessel in the eastern Pacific Ocean, killing two people accused of trafficking drugs.That strike ended a pause of more than two months in the campaign against alleged smugglers.The latest attack takes the number of people killed in US military boat strikes to at least 227 in 68 strikes since the Trump administration began targeting suspected traffickers nearly a year ago, according to news agency AP.The military has described those targeted as “narcoterrorists” and has said the vessels were operating along known smuggling routes in the Caribbean and the eastern Pacific.However, the military has generally not provided evidence publicly establishing that the targeted vessels were carrying drugs.In Tuesday's case, Southern Command provided no details about the vessel's cargo or the identities of the four people killed.The strikes have faced criticism from human rights organisations, including Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International, as well as independent UN experts, who have described the attacks as unlawful extrajudicial killings, according to Reuters.President Donald Trump has said the US is in “armed conflict” with Latin American cartels and has defended the strikes as necessary to stop drugs from reaching the United States and contributing to fatal overdoses.The administration has also sought agreements with Latin American governments to expand military operations against criminal groups on land.War secretary Pete Hegseth said during a visit to Panama this month that Colombia, Guatemala and Honduras had agreed to allow joint US military operations on their territory. Guatemala denied reaching such an agreement, while Ecuador launched similar missions with the US in March.The campaign has drawn scrutiny from Democratic lawmakers and military legal scholars, particularly over the legal basis for the strikes.The Pentagon's inspector general said in May that it planned to examine whether the military followed its established six-phase Joint Targeting Cycle when conducting the strikes.The review, however, was not intended to determine whether the attacks themselves were legally justified.The strikes have also raised questions over their effectiveness, with critics pointing out that fentanyl linked to many fatal US overdoses is generally trafficked over land from Mexico, where it is produced using chemicals imported from China and India.
Article Summary: US Southern Command posted a video of the operation on X, showing what appeared to be a moving boat followed by a flash after the strike. The military said intelligence had confirmed the vessel was actively involved in drug trafficking, but did not release evidence supporting the claim. The latest attack comes just two days after the US military struck another vessel in the eastern Pacific Ocean.

Article Title: She raised 11 children and was losing her hearing; despite a failed cochlear implant, this single mother earned her master's degree
Article Text:
PC: GCU

When hearing loss began to change Porter’s everyday life

Her cochlear implant opened a new door to sound, but complications followed

PC: ABC100

Graduate school happened alongside raising 11 children

PC: ABC100

Her graduation marked more than a degree after years of challenges

Turning her own struggle into hope for others

For Heather Porter, graduation day in Phoenix was not simply the end of a university course. It marked the close of several demanding years in which studying had to fit around a large family, foster care and a sudden change in the way she experienced the world.As reported by People, Porter received her master’s degree from Grand Canyon University on April 29, 2026, walking across the commencement stage in a purple gown. Among those watching was her seven-year-old daughter, Rebekah, who reached across the aisle to hold her mother’s hand during the ceremony.By then, Porter had already spent years adjusting to significant hearing loss and the complications that followed. She had also continued raising her children while completing her graduate studies online.Porter first noticed that something was wrong with her hearing while she was still an undergraduate. Conversations became harder to follow, and information that seemed straightforward to others could leave her struggling to keep up.As reported, the problem was eventually traced to an autoimmune condition affecting her inner ear.Her diagnosis came during the COVID-19 pandemic, a period when Porter was already dealing with the uncertainty of her changing hearing.The effect was not limited to classrooms or conversations. Porter described feeling increasingly cut off from people around her, including members of her own family. There was a period of grief as she adjusted to the possibility that her hearing would not return to what it had been.“I was struggling to understand things that other people understood easily,” she said of watching other people’s lips, as reported by Grand Canyon University News.Porter eventually received financial assistance that allowed her to have a cochlear implant. The device gave her another way to access sound, but her experience with it was far from straightforward.About a year and a half after the implant was fitted, it began malfunctioning. Porter experienced pain and other problems, and medical examinations showed that the device was failing. She was eventually told that electricity was leaking from the implant into her head. Surgery was required to replace it.The second implant became part of the routine she gradually built around her hearing. Porter also uses sign language, something that became particularly meaningful as she became more connected with the deaf and hard-of-hearing community.She has described learning sign language as an unexpected gift during a period when much of her life had been changing.Porter's university work was only one part of her life. She was raising a family of 11 children while completing her degree, including children who had joined the family through foster care and adoption.Her experience with foster care began when she and her then-husband took in a child and later decided to foster that child's three older siblings as well. Porter was 25 at the time.She later recalled that she did not want the siblings to be separated from one another, so the family took all four children in. Porter ultimately gave birth to six of her children. Her youngest, the 11th, was adopted while she was already in graduate school.That meant coursework and family responsibilities were running side by side. There were days when the demands of the degree felt difficult to manage, Porter acknowledged, and she has spoken about the tears that came during the programme. Still, she kept going.The commencement ceremony gave Porter a chance to mark the achievement with some of the people who had been part of the years it took to reach it.Images from the ceremony show her daughter Rebekah reaching towards her across the aisle, while another photograph captures Porter receiving her degree. Her sister, Annie Pearce, was also there and later embraced her after the ceremony. Pearce said Porter's familiarity with sign language and her existing connection with the deaf community had become an important part of how she handled the loss of her hearing.For Porter, the significance of the degree extends beyond having another qualification. She now hopes to use what she has learned in work with people who are hard of hearing.Porter plans to pursue work as a psychotherapist, with a particular interest in serving the hard-of-hearing community. Her own experience with hearing loss has given her a perspective that she hopes will be useful when working with people facing similar difficulties.She is also considering what could come after the master’s degree. A Ph.D. remains a possibility, as does teaching internationally. She summed up what she had taken from those years in a message about facing difficult circumstances without allowing them to define the rest of a person's life.“There is hope, no matter how low life feels,” Porter said.
Article Summary: Heather Porter received her master’s degree from Grand Canyon University on April 29, 2026, walking across the commencement stage in a purple gown. She was raising a family of 11 children while completing her degree, including children who had joined the family through foster care and adoption. Porter also uses sign language, something that became particularly meaningful as she became more connected with the deaf and hard-of-hearing community.

Article Title: How Nathan Straus transformed philanthropy and helped make pasteurised milk the safer choice for children
Article Text:
Image: Wikipedia

Nathan Straus turned his business experience towards philanthropy

Nathan Straus turned his business experience towards philanthropy (Image: Wikipedia)

The milk crisis that put children at risk

‘Retail giving’ made philanthropy practical

From a private campaign to a public-health standard

A forgotten legacy in American public health

Long before pasteurised milk became a routine part of American life, families in New York faced a serious and often overlooked public-health danger, contaminated milk. In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, raw milk could carry harmful pathogens and was especially dangerous for infants and young children. One wealthy businessman, Nathan Straus, used his fortune and business experience to tackle the problem in an unconventional way. Rather than simply donating money to charities, Straus created a system that combined philanthropy with practical retail distribution. He established milk laboratories and depots where pasteurised and refrigerated milk could be sold cheaply or provided free to families who could not afford it. His campaign eventually helped push pasteurisation into mainstream public-health policy and left a lasting mark on how Americans understood safe milk.Nathan Straus was born in 1848 and became wealthy through his involvement with major New York department stores, including Abraham and Straus and R.H. Macy and Co. After building his fortune, he and his wife, Lina Gutherz Straus, increasingly devoted their attention to philanthropic causes.The New York Public Library’s papers document his work in public health, milk pasteurisation, tuberculosis prevention and assistance to people affected by poverty and disasters. Straus’s approach to charity differed from the traditional model of simply handing out money. During the economic depression of the 1890s, he used his experience in merchandising to establish depots near New York’s poorer neighbourhoods, where essential goods could be provided at reduced prices. This practical approach later shaped his campaign for safer milk. His interest in milk became particularly personal and urgent. At the time, milk could spoil during transportation and storage, while contaminated supplies could expose children to dangerous diseases. Straus believed that improving the way milk was processed and distributed could save lives.In New York City during the 1890s, infant mortality was extraordinarily high. Raw milk was considered one of the major risks because it could contain disease-causing organisms, including bacteria associated with tuberculosis. Although scientists already understood that heating milk could destroy harmful microorganisms, pasteurisation was not yet universally accepted. Straus became one of its most determined advocates. In 1892, he established the Nathan Straus Pasteurized Milk Laboratory in New York at his own expense. The facility produced safer milk and helped establish a distribution network designed specifically to reach families in poorer parts of the city. His milk depots did more than sell a product. They made pasteurised and refrigerated milk accessible to people who might otherwise have had little choice but to purchase cheaper, potentially unsafe supplies. Some milk was sold below wholesale prices, while families unable to pay could receive it without charge. The NYPL collection includes records of the laboratory and its milk depots, including reports, brochures, instructions for mothers, infant-formula recipes and even coupons that could be redeemed at the depots.Straus’s method has since been described as a form of “retail giving” because it applied the efficiency of business to a social problem. Instead of creating a conventional charity dependent entirely on handouts, he developed a system capable of producing, pricing and distributing a health-protective product on a large scale. The approach also included education. Information was provided to mothers about infant care and the safe handling of milk, while doctors and nurses were involved in advising families. Straus supported efforts to demonstrate that pasteurisation could protect children without sacrificing the nutritional value of milk. His work expanded well beyond New York. According to historical accounts of his philanthropy, Straus and his wife ultimately helped establish hundreds of milk stations across numerous American cities. The NYPL collection records his efforts to promote pasteurisation through speeches, articles, medical and public-health meetings, and advocacy for legislation. The strategy was significant because it connected individual access to safer milk with a broader public-health campaign. Families could obtain pasteurised milk immediately, while policymakers and health professionals were exposed to evidence supporting wider adoption.Straus’s campaign unfolded at a time when public-health officials were increasingly concerned about infant mortality and infectious disease. His work helped demonstrate the practical benefits of making pasteurised milk available to communities that needed it most. The wider movement eventually contributed to changes in public policy. By the early 20th century, pasteurisation was gaining much greater acceptance among American health authorities, and governments increasingly moved towards requiring safer milk supplies. Straus did not single-handedly make American milk safe, but his efforts formed an important part of a much larger public-health transformation. His particular contribution was showing that philanthropy could operate at the point where a public-health problem actually affected people's daily lives: the purchase and consumption of food.Nathan Straus died in 1931, but the records preserved his legacy is striking because the solution he promoted now seems ordinary. Today, consumers generally expect commercially sold milk to have undergone safety controls that were far from universal when Straus began his campaign. What made his philanthropy distinctive was its practical focus. He did not simply ask how much money could be donated to a cause. He asked how a wealthy businessman could use the systems of production, distribution and retail to make a basic necessity safer and more affordable. That approach helped transform milk from a potential source of serious disease into a much safer staple for American families. In doing so, Straus showed how targeted philanthropy could influence not only individual lives but also the development of public-health practices that eventually reached far beyond the people his original milk stations served.
Article Summary: Nathan Straus turned his business experience towards philanthropy. He established milk laboratories and depots where pasteurised milk could be sold cheaply or provided free to families who could not afford it. His campaign eventually helped push pasteurisation into mainstream public-health policy and left a lasting mark on how Americans understood safe milk.

Article Title: Texas Roadhouse says claims of white employees discussing spitting in Black customers' food in a Facebook group are 'completely unfounded'
Article Text:
Texas Roadhouse said they investigated and found no such private Facebook group where white staff discuss about spitting in the food of Black guests.

Viral post deleted after creating outrage

Texas Roadhouse clapped back at the viral social media claim that its white servers were discussing spitting in Black customers' food in a private Facebook group as a hoax and confirmed that the claims based on which diners raised boycott calls were completely unfounded. The controversy started when an unverified claim originated on Facebook, allegedly from a user warning Black diners to avoid eating at Texas Roadhouse and Logan's Roadhouse. The post alleged that a secret Facebook group boasting over 400,000 white server members existed for the explicit purpose of organizing food contamination targeted at Black customers. Specific accusations claimed that servers were licking their fingers, spitting in saliva, and touching items like the chain's famous fresh rolls before serving them.The controversy escalated as the post went viral and customers called for a nationwide boycott."We are committed to creating an environment where every guest is treated with respect and unreasonable hospitality," Texas Roadhouse officials wrote responding to the outrage. "We do not tolerate discrimination, harassment or mistreatment of any kind, and we expect our Roadies to treat every guest with dignity and care."Texas Roadhouse brought in an independent third-party cybersecurity firm to trace the origins of the post. They confirmed there was no evidence of such a 400,000-member group existing, nor any record of food-tampering incidents linked to the claim.Travis Doster, chief communications officer of Texas Roadhouse, told USA TODAY that some social media users who defamed the chain retracted their statements after it was proved to be a hoax."There’s no video of any of our servers," he said. "There’s no video of anybody saying they have evidence. It’s very frustrating because it’s not true." He also suggested the culprit behind the post could be bots, or automated programs that make posts mimicking human engagement online. "There is zero credible evidence this is true,” he said. “This did not happen in any of our restaurants."The original Facebook post was deleted. It was allegedly shared in a Facebook group called "White and proud," where a user named Nancy Smith said they worked at an unidentified Texas Roadhouse location and was in a pact with other White servers at the restaurant to contaminate the food of Black guests.The user said this had been going on for a while, or at least since the April 2025 killing of 17-year-old Austin Metcalf by Black teenager Karmelo Anthony. Anthony has been sentenced to 35 years in prison for the stabbing.
Article Summary: Texas Roadhouse said they investigated and found no such private Facebook group where white staff discuss about spitting in the food of Black guests. The controversy started when an unverified claim originated on Facebook, allegedly from a user warning Black diners to avoid eating at Texas Roadhouse and Logan's Roadhouse.

Article Title: 'We got this wrong': Target says sorry for Halloween costume that looked like racist caricature, pulls it down from collection
Article Text:
Target said sorry for its Halloween costume (left) after backlash that it looked like caricature.

Internal email sent by chief merchandising officer

Target acknowledged and corrected its mistake after one of its children Hallowen costume triggered a massive outrage. The retain giant said it had pulled down the costume from sale after social media users pointed out that the circus clown evoked Blackface and minstrel shows."The $25 costume was listed as the “Kids’ Glows under Blacklight Circus Clown Halloween Costume Bodysuit” from Target’s Hyde & EEK! Boutique line. The design featured an orange-and-black clown outfit, black gloves and a dark face covering with an exaggerated smiling mouth. We still shopping at Target?" a social media post said, pointing out how problematic the Halloween costume was."As a company, we know we got this wrong, and we are deeply sorry. The costume is offensive and should never have been part of our assortment. It is no longer available for sale," Target said in its statement."We know this is especially hurtful for our Black guests, team members and partners. Removing the costume is an important first step, and the company is looking closely at how this happened and what needs to change to ensure this won’t happen again," the statement read.Social media was divided on whether it was an unintentional mistake."At this point, it's intentional. There is no way no one on the board doesn't know this is offensive," one wrote. "Target definitely did this intentionally. Their marketing team is trying to stir up controversy. Even bad publicity is STILL publicity," another wrote.Blackface is dark makeup worn to mimic the appearance of a Black person and especially to mock or ridicule Black people, according to Merriam-Webster.
